source_refs.note: Book p. 99: 6.5.1 Rule for nth term of a G.P., derivation of a_n = a1 r^(n-1)

items.title: 6.5.1 Rule for nth term of a G.P.

blocks.text:
Each term after the first term is an \(r\) multiple of its preceding term. Thus, we have,
\[a_2 = a_1 r = a_1 r^{2-1}\]
\[a_3 = a_2 r = (a_1 r)r\]
\[= a_1 r^{2} = a_1 r^{3-1}\]
\[a_4 = a_3 r = (a_1 r^{2})r\]
\[= a_1 r^{3} = a_1 r^{4-1}\]
\[\vdots\]

blocks.text_alt: a n equals a 1 times r to the power n minus 1

blocks.text: which is the general term of a G.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the power \(n - 1\) and not \(n\)? Look at the pattern: in \(a_2\) the power of \(r\) is 1, in \(a_3\) it is 2, in \(a_4\) it is 3. The power is always one less than the position, because from the first term to the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term we multiply by \(r\) only \(n - 1\) times (there are \(n - 1\) jumps between \(n\) terms).
Compare with the A.P.: \(a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\). There \(d\) is added \(n - 1\) times, so it is multiplied by \(n - 1\); here \(r\) is multiplied \(n - 1\) times, so it is raised to the power \(n - 1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick illustration of the rule: for \(a_1 = 2\) and \(r = 3\),
\[a_5 = 2 \cdot 3^{5-1} = 2 \cdot 81 = 162\]
Writing the terms out confirms it: \(2, 6, 18, 54, 162\). The formula gives any term directly, even \(a_{20}\), without listing all the terms before it.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The formula links four quantities \(a_1, r, n, a_n\); given any three, the fourth can be found. When \(r\) is negative or a fraction, keep it in brackets: \((-2)^{7}\), \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{6}\). A negative \(r\) raised to an even power is positive, to an odd power negative.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. General term of a G.P.: \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\).
2. The power of \(r\) is one less than the term's position.
3. Only \(r\) is raised to the power; \(a_1\) multiplies the result.
4. Four quantities \(a_1, r, n, a_n\): any three give the fourth.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(a_n = a_1 r^{n}\): the power is \(n - 1\).
2. Writing \((a_1 r)^{n-1}\): only \(r\) is raised to the power.
3. Writing \(-2^{7}\) for \((-2)^{7}\) when \(r = -2\): without brackets the sign is lost from the power.
